entities.name: Gopala III
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gopala IV, initially identified as Gopala III in earlier historical accounts, ascended to the throne of the Pala Empire in the Bengal region of the Indian subcontinent around 1129 CE, succeeding his father, King Kumarapala. His reign, which lasted until his death in 1144 CE, marked a period of continued contraction for the once-dominant Pala dynasty, as various regional powers, most notably the resurgent Sena dynasty, intensified their territorial encroachments and challenged Pala suzerainty. Despite the diminishing territorial control, Gopala IV's rule is evidenced by significant epigraphic and manuscript discoveries, providing valuable insights into the political and cultural landscape of 12th-century Bengal.

During his fifteen-year tenure, Gopala IV struggled to maintain the integrity of the Pala realm against the rising power of the Senas under Vijayasena, who systematically annexed territories in eastern Bengal. While specific military campaigns or grand architectural projects attributed directly to Gopala IV are scarce, his reign is notably documented by a manuscript of the *Pancharaksha* text, dated to the 15th regnal year (c. 1144 CE), which is now preserved in the British Library. This manuscript, inscribed during his rule, underscores the continued patronage of Buddhist scholarship and art, even as the political fortunes of the Pala kings waned.

The legacy of Gopala IV is primarily understood as part of the twilight of the Pala Empire, a once-mighty Buddhist kingdom that had shaped the cultural and political contours of Bengal and Bihar for centuries. His inability to halt the territorial losses set the stage for the eventual dissolution of Pala authority, paving the way for the complete ascendancy of the Sena dynasty across most of Bengal. This transition profoundly impacted the region's socio-political structure, shifting from a Buddhist-patronizing empire to a Hindu-centric kingdom, altering the trajectory of local religious and artistic patronage.
